questions.question: Given that $\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-7\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\4\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\overrightarrow{AB}$?
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\4\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}2\\-7\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\11\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: The polynomial $p(x)=x^3-6x^2+32$ has one repeated zero of multiplicity 2 at $x=\alpha$. What is the value of $\alpha$?
questions.answer: A double zero satisfies $p(\alpha)=0$ and $p'(\alpha)=0$. $p'(x)=3x^2-12x=3x(x-4)$, so $\alpha=0$ or $4$. $p(0)=32\neq0$, while $p(4)=64-96+32=0$. So $\alpha=4$.

questions.question:
A solid of revolution is to be formed by rotating the region bounded by the $x$-axis and the curve $y=\cos 3x$ between $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ about the $x$-axis, as shown in the diagram.

Which of the following gives the volume of the solid of revolution formed?
questions.answer:
$$V=\pi\int_{-\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos^2 3x\,dx=2\pi\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos^2 3x\,dx\quad(\cos^2 3x\text{ is even})$$
$$=2\pi\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\tfrac12(1+\cos 6x)\,dx=\pi\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(1+\cos 6x)\,dx.$$

questions.question:
The projection of $\mathbf{u}$ onto $\mathbf{v}$ is given by $\left(\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\right)\mathbf{v}$.

The diagram shows points $A$, $B$ and $C$, where $\overrightarrow{AB}=3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$.

Which of the following is the projection of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ onto $\overrightarrow{AC}$?
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=3(-1)+1(-1)=-4$ and $|\overrightarrow{AC}|^2=2$, so the projection is $\dfrac{-4}{2}(-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})=2(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$. (Quick check: the angle at $A$ is obtuse, so the projection must point opposite to $\overrightarrow{AC}$ — only C does.)

questions.question: Five different schools send two prefects each to attend a conference. The group of 10 is to be seated at a circular table. In how many ways can the prefects be seated if prefects from the same school are to be seated together?
questions.answer: Treat each school's pair as one unit: 5 units around a circular table can be arranged in $4!$ ways. Each pair can be ordered in $2!=2$ ways, giving $2^5$. Total $=2^5\times4!$.

questions.question: You are given that $f(x)$ is a one-to-one function defined for $x\in(-\infty,\infty)$. Which of the following functions cannot have an inverse?
questions.answer: $f(|x|)$ is always even: $f(|-a|)=f(|a|)$, so it takes the same value at $x=a$ and $x=-a$ and fails the horizontal line test — it can never have an inverse. The others can be one-to-one (e.g. for $f(x)=e^x$ all three are).

questions.question: How many distinct solutions are there to the equation $\sin x+\sin 3x=\sin 2x$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$?
questions.answer:
$\sin 3x+\sin x=\sin(2x+x)+\sin(2x-x)=2\sin 2x\cos x$. So $2\sin 2x\cos x=\sin 2x$, i.e. $\sin 2x(2\cos x-1)=0$.

$\sin 2x=0$: $x=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2},2\pi$ (5 solutions). $\cos x=\frac12$: $x=\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{5\pi}{3}$ (2 more, all distinct). Total 7.

questions.question: Which graph represents the function $y=\tan^{-1}(\tan x)$?
questions.answer: $\tan x$ is defined for all $x\neq\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi$ and has period $\pi$; $\tan^{-1}$ has range $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$. On $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $y=x$, and the graph repeats every $\pi$: a sawtooth of parallel segments of gradient 1 with open circles at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi$. This is graph B.

questions.question:
It is known that the function $f(x)$ is one-to-one and continuous for all real $x$. Let $g(x)=f^{-1}(x)$.

Which of the following statements MUST be true for any value of $x$ where $f'(x)$ and $g'(x)$ are both defined?
questions.answer: A continuous one-to-one function is either increasing everywhere or decreasing everywhere, and its inverse is monotonic in the same direction. So $f'(x)$ and $g'(x)$ always have the same sign, giving $f'(x)g'(x)>0$ (where neither is zero). B is false in general because $g'(x)=\dfrac{1}{f'(g(x))}$, not $\dfrac{1}{f'(x)}$.

questions.question: Which statement is always true for real numbers $a$ and $b$ where $0\le a<b\le 1$?
questions.answer: Let $f(x)=\cos^{-1}x-\sin^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}x-\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\cos^{-1}x\right)=2\cos^{-1}x-\frac{\pi}{2}$. Since $\cos^{-1}x$ is decreasing on $[0,1]$, so is $f$, hence $f(a)>f(b)$. (A is reversed since $\cos^{-1}$ is decreasing; C is reversed since $\cos$ is positive and decreasing on $[0,1]$; D fails, e.g. $a=0,b=1$: $0>\sin1\cos1$ is false.)

questions.question:
The parametric equations of a line are

$$x=2-5t,\qquad y=3t+1.$$

Find the Cartesian equation of this line in the form $y=mx+c$.
Find the inverse function, $f^{-1}(x)$, of the function $f(x)=e^{2x}-1$.
questions.answer:
Interchange $x$ and $y$: $x=e^{2y}-1$, so $e^{2y}=x+1$, $2y=\ln(x+1)$.

$$f^{-1}(x)=\frac12\ln(x+1)\quad(x>-1).$$

questions.question:
Consider the polynomial $P(x)=x^3-2x^2-7x-4$.

Show that $x+1$ is a factor of $P(x)$ and hence find $P(x)$ in fully factorised form.
questions.answer:
$P(-1)=-1-2+7-4=0$, so by the factor theorem $(x+1)$ is a factor.

Dividing, $P(x)=(x+1)(x^2-3x-4)=(x+1)(x+1)(x-4)$, so

$$P(x)=(x+1)^2(x-4).$$

questions.question: Solve $\dfrac{2x}{3-x}\le 4$.
questions.answer:
$x\neq3$. Multiply both sides by $(3-x)^2>0$:

$$2x(3-x)\le4(3-x)^2$$
$$4(3-x)^2-2x(3-x)\ge0$$
$$(3-x)\left[4(3-x)-2x\right]\ge0$$
$$(3-x)(12-6x)\ge0\;\Rightarrow\;6(x-3)(x-2)\ge0.$$

This upward parabola is $\ge0$ for $x\le2$ or $x\ge3$; excluding $x=3$:

$$x\le2\quad\text{or}\quad x>3.$$

questions.question: Find the coefficient of $x^{10}$ in the expansion of $\left(\dfrac{2}{x}-x^3\right)^6$.
questions.answer:
General term: $\displaystyle\binom{6}{r}\left(\frac2x\right)^{6-r}(-x^3)^r=\binom6r2^{6-r}(-1)^r x^{4r-6}$.

For $x^{10}$: $4r-6=10\Rightarrow r=4$.

Coefficient $=\displaystyle\binom64 2^2(-1)^4=15\times4=60$.

questions.question: Use mathematical induction to prove that $4n^3-n$ is divisible by 3 for all integers $n\ge1$.
questions.answer:
**Base case** $n=1$: $4(1)^3-1=3=3\times1$, divisible by 3. True.

**Assume** true for $n=k$: $4k^3-k=3A$ for some integer $A$.

**Prove** for $n=k+1$:
$$\begin{aligned}4(k+1)^3-(k+1)&=4(k^3+3k^2+3k+1)-k-1\\&=(4k^3-k)+12k^2+12k+3\\&=3A+3(4k^2+4k+1)\\&=3(A+4k^2+4k+1),\end{aligned}$$
which is divisible by 3 since $A+4k^2+4k+1$ is an integer.

Hence, by mathematical induction, $4n^3-n$ is divisible by 3 for all integers $n\ge1$.

questions.question: Express $3\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x$ in the form $2\sqrt3\sin(x+\alpha)$, where $0<\alpha<2\pi$.
questions.answer:
$2\sqrt3\sin(x+\alpha)=(2\sqrt3\cos\alpha)\sin x+(2\sqrt3\sin\alpha)\cos x$. Equating coefficients:

$$\cos\alpha=\frac{3}{2\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\qquad \sin\alpha=\frac{-\sqrt3}{2\sqrt3}=-\frac12.$$

So $\alpha$ is in the 4th quadrant: $\alpha=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$, and

$$3\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x=2\sqrt3\sin\left(x+\frac{11\pi}{6}\right).$$

questions.question:
It is given that $3\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x=2\sqrt3\sin\left(x+\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\right)$.

Hence, or otherwise, solve $3\sin x=\sqrt3\cos x-\sqrt3$, where $0\le x<2\pi$.
questions.answer:
$3\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x=-\sqrt3$, so $2\sqrt3\sin\left(x+\frac{11\pi}{6}\right)=-\sqrt3$, i.e. $\sin\left(x+\frac{11\pi}{6}\right)=-\frac12$.

With $\frac{11\pi}{6}\le x+\frac{11\pi}{6}<\frac{23\pi}{6}$: $x+\frac{11\pi}{6}=\frac{11\pi}{6}$ or $\frac{19\pi}{6}$.

$$x=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=\frac{4\pi}{3}.$$

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}\frac{8x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx$ using the substitution $x=\sin\theta$.
questions.answer:
$x=\sin\theta$, $dx=\cos\theta\,d\theta$. When $x=0$, $\theta=0$; when $x=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$. For $0\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{3}$, $\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}\frac{8x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\frac{8\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}\cos\theta\,d\theta=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}8\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\\&=4\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}(1-\cos2\theta)\,d\theta=4\left[\theta-\tfrac12\sin2\theta\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\&=4\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)=\frac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt3.\end{aligned}$$

questions.question:
Charles is a member of an elite racing group of 11 people. A team of 5 people is to be formed from the group. Use a combinatorial argument in this context to prove that

$$\binom{11}{5}=\binom{10}{4}+\binom{10}{5}.$$
questions.answer:
**LHS:** the number of teams of 5 chosen from 11 people is $\binom{11}{5}$.

**RHS:** count the same teams by whether Charles is in the team.
- Charles is in the team: choose the other 4 members from the remaining 10 people: $\binom{10}{4}$ ways.
- Charles is not in the team: choose all 5 from the other 10 people: $\binom{10}{5}$ ways.

These cases are disjoint and cover every team, so $\binom{11}{5}=\binom{10}{4}+\binom{10}{5}$.

questions.question: By sketching a graph, or otherwise, solve $(|x|-1)(|x|-2)=6$.
questions.answer:
Let $f(x)=(x-1)(x-2)$; the equation is $f(|x|)=6$.

Solve $f(x)=6$: $x^2-3x+2=6\Rightarrow x^2-3x-4=0\Rightarrow(x-4)(x+1)=0$, so $x=-1$ or $4$.

The graph of $y=f(|x|)$ is the part of $y=f(x)$ for $x\ge0$ reflected in the $y$-axis, so only the solution $x=4\ (\ge0)$ survives, together with its reflection. (Equivalently $|x|=4$ or $|x|=-1$, the latter impossible.)

$$x=\pm4.$$

questions.question:
Let $f(x)=\tan^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\right)$, for $x>-1$.

Show that $f(x)=k$, where $k$ is a real number.
questions.answer:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{1}{1+x^2}-\frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{x-1}{x+1}\right)^2}\cdot\frac{(x+1)-(x-1)}{(x+1)^2}\\&=\frac{1}{1+x^2}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^2+(x-1)^2}\\&=\frac{1}{1+x^2}-\frac{2}{2x^2+2}=0.\end{aligned}$$
Since $f'(x)=0$ for all $x>-1$ (an interval), $f(x)$ is constant: $f(x)=k$.

questions.question:
Let $f(x)=\tan^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\right)$, for $x>-1$. It is known that $f(x)=k$ for some real constant $k$.

Find the value of $k$.

A particle is moving on the curve with equation

$$y=2\sin^{-1}3x,\qquad -\frac13\le x\le\frac13.$$

The particle has coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$, where distances are measured in metres and time in seconds.

At $t=T$, the $y$ coordinate of the particle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ m and the $y$ coordinate is increasing at a rate of 2 m/s.

Find the exact rate at which the $x$ coordinate of the particle is changing at $t=T$.
questions.answer:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=2\cdot\frac{3}{\sqrt{1-9x^2}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{1-9x^2}}.$$
When $y=\frac{\pi}{3}$: $\sin^{-1}3x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, so $3x=\frac12$, $x=\frac16$.

Then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{1-\frac14}}=\dfrac{6}{\sqrt3/2}=\dfrac{12}{\sqrt3}$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dy}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{12}$.

$$\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{dx}{dy}\cdot\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{\sqrt3}{12}\times2=\frac{\sqrt3}{6}\ \text{m/s}.$$

questions.question:
At a particular high school, 17 students, including Xavi and Yuri, are enrolled to study Mathematics Extension 1. There are three Mathematics Extension 1 classes with a maximum class size of 6. Each class is taught by a different teacher.

Students are randomly assigned into classes. Find the number of ways the classes can be assigned to teachers such that Xavi and Yuri are in the same class.
questions.answer:
With 17 students and at most 6 per class, the only possible class sizes are $6,6,5$.

**Case 1: Xavi and Yuri are in a class of 6.** Choose the other 4 members of their class from the remaining 15, then 6 of the remaining 11 for the other class of 6; the last 5 form the class of 5. The three (distinct) classes can be given to the three teachers in $3!$ ways:
$$\binom{15}{4}\binom{11}{6}\binom55\times3!=1365\times462\times6=3\,783\,780.$$
**Case 2: Xavi and Yuri are in the class of 5.** Choose the other 3 from 15, then split the remaining 12 into two classes of 6 (divide by $2!$ as these two groups are interchangeable before teachers are assigned), then assign teachers in $3!$ ways:
$$\frac{\binom{15}{3}\binom{12}{6}\binom66\times3!}{2!}=\frac{455\times924\times6}{2}=1\,261\,260.$$
**Total:** $3\,783\,780+1\,261\,260=5\,045\,040$.

questions.question:
A solid trophy is to be made by rotating the shaded region shown around the $y$-axis. The region is bounded by the $y$-axis, the $x$-axis, the line $y=2$, and the curves $y=\sqrt{5-\dfrac{1}{x^4}}$ (for $0\le y\le1$) and $y=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{x^2}-1}$ (for $1\le y\le2$), which meet at $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2},1\right)$.

Show that the volume of the trophy is $\dfrac{\pi^2}{4}$ units$^3$.
questions.answer:
Express $x^2$ in terms of $y$ for each curve:

- $y^2=5-\dfrac{1}{x^4}\Rightarrow x^4=\dfrac{1}{5-y^2}\Rightarrow x^2=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5-y^2}}$ (used for $0\le y\le1$).
- $y^2=\dfrac{1}{x^2}-1\Rightarrow x^2=\dfrac{1}{1+y^2}$ (used for $1\le y\le2$).

$$V_1=\pi\int_0^1\frac{dy}{\sqrt{5-y^2}}=\pi\left[\sin^{-1}\frac{y}{\sqrt5}\right]_0^1=\pi\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt5}$$
$$V_2=\pi\int_1^2\frac{dy}{1+y^2}=\pi\left[\tan^{-1}y\right]_1^2=\pi\left(\tan^{-1}2-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$$
So $V=\pi\left(\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt5}+\tan^{-1}2-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$.

In a right-angled triangle with legs 2 and 1 and hypotenuse $\sqrt5$, the angle $\theta$ opposite the side 1 has $\sin\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}$ and the other acute angle $\varphi$ has $\tan\varphi=2$. Since $\theta+\varphi=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt5}+\tan^{-1}2=\frac{\pi}{2}$. Hence
$$V=\pi\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{\pi^2}{4}\text{ units}^3.$$

questions.question:
In triangle $ABC$, $D$ lies on $AC$ such that $\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac14\overrightarrow{AC}$, and $E$ lies on $BC$ such that $\overrightarrow{BE}=\frac13\overrightarrow{BC}$. $F$ lies on $BD$ such that $FE\parallel AC$.

Show that $\overrightarrow{FE}=\overrightarrow{FB}+\dfrac13\overrightarrow{BC}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{FE}=\overrightarrow{FB}+\overrightarrow{BE}=\overrightarrow{FB}+\dfrac13\overrightarrow{BC}$.

questions.question:
In triangle $ABC$, $D$ lies on $AC$ such that $\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac14\overrightarrow{AC}$, and $E$ lies on $BC$ such that $\overrightarrow{BE}=\frac13\overrightarrow{BC}$. $F$ lies on $BD$ such that $FE\parallel AC$.

It is known that $\overrightarrow{FE}=\overrightarrow{FB}+\dfrac13\overrightarrow{BC}$.

Let $\overrightarrow{FE}=k\overrightarrow{DC}$. Use vector methods to show that $\overrightarrow{FE}=\overrightarrow{AD}$.
questions.answer:
$$k\overrightarrow{DC}=\overrightarrow{FB}+\tfrac13\overrightarrow{BC}$$
$$k\left(\overrightarrow{DB}+\overrightarrow{BC}\right)=\overrightarrow{FB}+\tfrac13\overrightarrow{BC}$$
Since $F$ lies on $BD$, $\overrightarrow{DB}=\lambda\overrightarrow{FB}$ for some scalar $\lambda$:
$$k\lambda\overrightarrow{FB}+k\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{FB}+\tfrac13\overrightarrow{BC}.$$
$\overrightarrow{FB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ are not parallel, so equating coefficients of $\overrightarrow{BC}$: $k=\frac13$, i.e. $\overrightarrow{DC}=3\overrightarrow{FE}$.

Also $\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac14\overrightarrow{AC}=\frac14\left(\overrightarrow{AD}+\overrightarrow{DC}\right)$, so $\frac34\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac14\overrightarrow{DC}$, i.e. $\overrightarrow{DC}=3\overrightarrow{AD}$.

Therefore $3\overrightarrow{AD}=3\overrightarrow{FE}$, so $\overrightarrow{FE}=\overrightarrow{AD}$.

questions.question:
The polynomial $p(x)=x^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has stationary points at $x=\alpha$ and $x=\beta$, where $\alpha\neq\beta$.

Show that $b^2>3c$.
questions.answer:
$p'(x)=3x^2+2bx+c$. Two distinct stationary points means $p'(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots, so $\Delta>0$:
$$(2b)^2-4(3)(c)>0\;\Rightarrow\;4b^2>12c\;\Rightarrow\;b^2>3c.$$

questions.question:
The polynomial $p(x)=x^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has stationary points at $x=\alpha$ and $x=\beta$, where $\alpha\neq\beta$.

You are given that $m^3-n^3=(m-n)(m^2+mn+n^2)$. (Do NOT prove this.)

Show that $\dfrac{p(\alpha)-p(\beta)}{\alpha-\beta}=\dfrac29\left(3c-b^2\right)$.
questions.answer:
$$\begin{aligned}p(\alpha)-p(\beta)&=(\alpha^3-\beta^3)+b(\alpha^2-\beta^2)+c(\alpha-\beta)\\&=(\alpha-\beta)\left[(\alpha^2+\alpha\beta+\beta^2)+b(\alpha+\beta)+c\right].\end{aligned}$$
$\alpha,\beta$ are the roots of $p'(x)=3x^2+2bx+c=0$, so $\alpha+\beta=-\frac{2b}{3}$ and $\alpha\beta=\frac c3$. Then
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{p(\alpha)-p(\beta)}{\alpha-\beta}&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-\alpha\beta+b(\alpha+\beta)+c\\&=\frac{4b^2}{9}-\frac c3-\frac{2b^2}{3}+c\\&=\frac{2c}{3}-\frac{2b^2}{9}=\frac29\left(3c-b^2\right).\end{aligned}$$

questions.question:
The polynomial $p(x)=x^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has stationary points at $x=\alpha$ and $x=\beta$, where $\alpha\neq\beta$.

It is known that $b^2>3c$ and that $\dfrac{p(\alpha)-p(\beta)}{\alpha-\beta}=\dfrac29\left(3c-b^2\right)$.

Hence, or otherwise, find the relationship between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $p(\alpha)>p(\beta)$.
questions.answer:
Since $b^2>3c$, the right-hand side $\frac29(3c-b^2)<0$. If $p(\alpha)>p(\beta)$, the numerator $p(\alpha)-p(\beta)>0$, so for the quotient to be negative we need $\alpha-\beta<0$:

$$\alpha<\beta.$$

(Graphically: a monic cubic with two stationary points has its local maximum to the left of its local minimum, so $p(\alpha)>p(\beta)$ means $\alpha$ is the maximum and $\beta$ the minimum, i.e. $\alpha<\beta$.)

questions.question:
Particle $A$ is projected from the origin with initial speed $V$ m s$^{-1}$ at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal plane. The position vector of particle $A$, $t$ seconds after it is projected, is given by

$$\mathbf{r}_A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Vt\cos\theta\\ Vt\sin\theta-\frac12gt^2\end{pmatrix}.\quad\text{(Do NOT prove this.)}$$

Show that the velocity vector of particle $A$ is given by $\mathbf{v}_A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\\ V\sin\theta-gt\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.answer: $$\mathbf{v}_A(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{r}_A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\\ V\sin\theta-2\cdot\frac12gt\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\\ V\sin\theta-gt\end{pmatrix}.$$

questions.question:
Particle $A$ is projected from the origin with initial speed $V$ m s$^{-1}$ at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal plane. The position vector of particle $A$, $t$ seconds after it is projected, is given by

$$\mathbf{r}_A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Vt\cos\theta\\ Vt\sin\theta-\frac12gt^2\end{pmatrix}.\quad\text{(Do NOT prove this.)}$$

The velocity vector of particle $A$ is $\mathbf{v}_A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\\ V\sin\theta-gt\end{pmatrix}$.

After $T$ seconds, particle $B$ is projected from the origin with the same initial speed and angle as particle $A$. The position vector of particle $B$ is given by

$$\mathbf{r}_B(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V(t-T)\cos\theta\\ V(t-T)\sin\theta-\frac12g(t-T)^2\end{pmatrix},\ t\ge T.\quad\text{(Do NOT prove this.)}$$

Show that the particles will never travel in perpendicular directions at any time $t$ if $T<\dfrac{2V\cos\theta}{g}$.
questions.answer:
$\mathbf{v}_B(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\\ V\sin\theta-g(t-T)\end{pmatrix}$.

The directions are perpendicular when $\mathbf{v}_A\cdot\mathbf{v}_B=0$:
$$V^2\cos^2\theta+(V\sin\theta-gt)\left(V\sin\theta-g(t-T)\right)=0$$
$$V^2\cos^2\theta+V^2\sin^2\theta-gV\sin\theta(t-T)-gVt\sin\theta+g^2t(t-T)=0$$
$$g^2t^2-\left(2gV\sin\theta+g^2T\right)t+\left(V^2+gVT\sin\theta\right)=0.$$
They are never perpendicular if this quadratic in $t$ has no real solution, i.e. $\Delta<0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\left(2gV\sin\theta+g^2T\right)^2-4g^2\left(V^2+gVT\sin\theta\right)&<0\\4g^2V^2\sin^2\theta+4g^3VT\sin\theta+g^4T^2-4g^2V^2-4g^3VT\sin\theta&<0\\g^4T^2&<4g^2V^2(1-\sin^2\theta)\\T^2&<\frac{4V^2\cos^2\theta}{g^2}.\end{aligned}$$
Since $T>0$ and $\cos\theta>0$, this holds exactly when $T<\dfrac{2V\cos\theta}{g}$. So if $T<\dfrac{2V\cos\theta}{g}$ there is no time at which the particles travel in perpendicular directions.
